    How Fresh York reacted to postponement of Macy's parade.

    Since Fresh York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

    "It was jarring," remarked Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make latest arrangements for over 500 people.

    Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (Â£267,000) in just a few hours.

    Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

    On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers declared the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

    The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

    The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

    Recent findings suggest that each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

    Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather.

    Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving.

    Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.

    "My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he remarked.

    "Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?".

    The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of Newly introduced York City during the holidays.

    There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the Fresh York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.

    Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.

    "The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich noted, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.

    He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".

    "We have a lot to be thankful for this Thanksgiving.".

    Some groups were not able to maneuver as easily. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band is one of those missing out, due to a schedule conflict on Saturday.

    ââThis canât be happeningâ,â Rina Browder, mother of a snare drummer in the band, told local news, describing the bandâs reactions.

    Industry observers note that "They were devastated. They've worked so hard for this. So many practices.".

    The Pride of Pearland Marching Band from Texas - pictured rehearsing earlier this week - noted it raised hundreds of thousands of dollars.

    Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the NÄ Koa AliÊ»i HawaiÊ»i All-State Marching Band, noted it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.

    In a recent development, speaking to the BBC on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.

    The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to Latest York.

    "Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.

    According to recent reports, but the musicians sprang into action swiftly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".

    The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he remarked.

    Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it needed to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.

    "Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Professor Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.

    It has been revealed that by Friday, 3,500 donors had stepped up to help the 410 students and their travel party. "This is truly phenomenal," mentioned Houser.

    While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain brought by the storm to eastern areas of the US.

    #150343. Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1324 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype.
    • GTA VI debuted as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).
    • The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.

    GTA VI debuted as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).

    The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.

    Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda, who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.”.

    Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids.

    “We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder, managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent organization Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.

    That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI.

    It has been revealed that “We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.”.

    Industry observers note that as millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public. At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s $81.3 billion IPO. At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time.

    But when the Anthropic team rang the bell on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large.

    Recent findings suggest that the AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star. The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas. Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out.

    This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with mind-numbing slop on YouTube, lawyers cite nonexistent cases in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “Year of Efficiency.” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade.

    The final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be hard to distinguish gameplay footage from real life. These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating new landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities.

    In a recent development, the video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI. Google’s Project Genie, which debuted earlier this year, allows consumers to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM. The stock prices of several video game companies faltered around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers.

    “The notion that somehow fresh tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick stated at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.”.

    Zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though. On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.”.

    Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI.

    In a recent development, “You won’t even have to ask,” Musk wrote on X. “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.”.

    In a recent development, this is the paradox of “Grandthropic” week. GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice). GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate.

    According to recent reports, “Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder said. “Creative output requires deletion, right? Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion. And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.”.

    GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms.

    In a recent development, the game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor. People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest missions involve driving around doing errands and putting up drywall to make your girlfriend happy. Don’t worry — there are still car chases and shootouts — but in a moment when AI feels suffocating, GTA VI is such an artistic achievement that it is reaching audiences that don’t even like violent video games.

    The ultimate fantasy of GTA VI is no longer to role-play as a criminal — the fantasy is just taking your time to relish the mundane and explore an expansive world that developers were given the time and space to perfect.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that every year has a Prime Day—some years even have two Prime Days!—where we celebrate the life and achievements of the greatest leader the Autobots have ever known: the inimitable Optimus Prime. But just as every dawn is twinned by a dusk that steals its light, so too did Optimus Prime’s bright spark fade, extinguished by the foul hand of Megatron during the Great Decepticon Incursion of 2005.

    It is a day that lives in infamy forever, and we all know the tale—how the evil Megatron (cursed be the flow of his energon!) commandeered an Autobot shuttle, cruelly murdered its crew, and rolled out a cowardly surprise attack against Autobot City—a initiative utterly bereft of honor, as was so typical of Megatron’s schemes. Even as individual Autobots strove to secure Autobot City—heroes, all of them!—hope began to fade under an onslaught that included an attack by the fearsome Devastator, against which there appeared to be no defense.

    And then, at the precipice of disaster, Optimus Prime made the fateful declaration whose words still ring out to this day: “Megatron must be stopped, no matter the cost.” The fearless Autobot transformed, rolled out, and got the job done—even though that cost was high. Many brave Autobots besides Optimus Prime lost their lives during the fighting. It was truly a dark day, a black day—and so, every year on the Friday after Thanksgiving, we pause to remember the noble sacrifices made by Prime and by so many others. This is why today is known as Black Friday.

    Recent findings suggest that and how do we remember those Autobots who joined the Allspark so that we could live in freedom? Optimus Prime was succeeded by Rodimus Prime, who defeated the darkness and brought hope back to all Cybertron. (We don’t talk about the brief Ultra Magnus-led Prime Interregnal Period.) Even Optimus Prime himself wouldn’t stay dead for very long—his own glorious and perhaps narratively inevitable resurrection would occur not that long after. Indeed, we will be celebrating those grand events in just a couple of days, on Cybertron Monday (or just “Cyber Monday” for short), with more shopping!

    In a recent development, oura will be dropping support for Android 11 on December 8th, 2026, and users may not have access to all of their data if they don’t upgrade to Android 12 or higher before the deadline. The support page now reads:.

    Oura will drop support for Android 11 on December 8, 2026. If you are using an Android device, be sure to upgrade to Android 12 or higher to ensure no loss of data or features. If you decide not to upgrade, you may still be able to use some limited historical Oura App features. Please note that if you do upgrade your smartphone system later, your historical Oura data will not carry over.

    It has been revealed that companies often end support for older OSes, and Android 11 came out in 2020, so it’s getting a bit long in the tooth. Normally, though, this just means missing out on new features or bug fixes. Losing historical health data is more surprising, and Oura offers no explanation for why the data wouldn’t be preserved. If you’ve been procrastinating updating your phone, or hemming and hawing about replacing it, now might be the time to finally take the plunge.

    If you’re not quite ready to, at least make sure to head to the membership hub and export your data so you have a backup ahead of December 8th.

    Germany news: Lawmakers approve debt-laden 2027 budget

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germany is talking about on Friday, 27 November.
    • The checkered or arctic skipper, carterocephalus palaemon, has been named the 2027 butterfly of the year by BUND, the German Federation for the Environment and Nature Conservation.
    • As so often, the animal has a more literal and descriptive moniker in German, where it's known as the gelbwürfelige Dickkopffalter, or "yellow-checked thick-headed butterfly" — an homage to two of its most distinguishing features, its coloration and its large head.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germany is talking about on Friday, 27 November. Catch up on yesterday's news here.

    The checkered or arctic skipper, carterocephalus palaemon, has been named the 2027 butterfly of the year by BUND, the German Federation for the Environment and Nature Conservation.

    As so often, the animal has a more literal and descriptive moniker in German, where it's known as the gelbwürfelige Dickkopffalter, or "yellow-checked thick-headed butterfly" — an homage to two of its most distinguishing features, its coloration and its large head.

    BUND said that with its choice for 2027 it wanted to "raise awareness about the loss of valuable water-based ecosystems." It said that the loss of transitional areas between woods and open land with long grasses were crucial to both the butterfly and the caterpillars and were being lost.

    Recent findings suggest that "Forest and path edges are often mowed short. With this, the butterflies' feeding and wintering locations are lost. The climate crisis is also weighing on the checkered skipper: for the caterpillars' development, carterocephalus palaemon needs damp living spaces or at least a damp microclimate.".

    The species is not classified as endangered in Germany at present, but its numbers are in decline.

    One of the two Iraqi nationals arrested yesterday on suspicion of plotting an attack on Cologne synagogue had been placed on a list of people who should leave the country in 2024, according to North Rhine-Westphalia's Refugee Ministry.

    It has been revealed that the 34-year-old Ameer J. appears to have been placed on a list of people from Iraq who were nominally supposed to leave the country but who were granted a dispensation to stay known in German as a "Duldung," stemming from the word for tolerate.

    "The first information available to us indicates that one of the two suspects was included on the so-called Unna List that our ministry compiled in the autumn of 2024," NRW's Refugee Minister Verena Schäfer told regional broadcaster WDR.

    This followed similar reporting in German media, including from the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper and Der Spiegel.

    WDR cited authorities in the city of Cologne as saying the decision to tolerate the man staying was based on him having regular employment at the time, and because he was not in need of replacement passport documentation given his valid Iraqi passport.

    The regional broadcaster also reported, citing security sources, that the alleged Islamist had been under observation for several months, partly after he was noticed by investigators looking into an attack on a Jewish site in Munich in April of 2026.

    Industry observers note that the two men arrested on Thrusday were accused of plotting attacks against the synagogue in Cologne and one other, unnamed, European city. They are thought to have been working for or in conjunction with a pro-Iranian terrorist group. Prosecutors mentioned that, for reasons that were not yet clear, the planned attacks were not ultimately carried out.

    French hard-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon visited Berlin on Friday, and said he sees "a need for a thorough overhaul of the Franco-German relationship.".

    Melenchon, who is hoping the radical economic platform he's championed for decades in France might finally resonate with voters in the vacuum left by Emmanuel Macron as he hits term limit in April's presidential elections, remarked he opposed the German government's spending and defense policies.

    "I am hostile to the liberal [economic] policy of German governments that dominates the European Union," the 75-year-old stated.

    Melenchon advocates drastically increasing public spending in France, already the much more debt-laden of the EU's top two economies, and canceling French debt held by the European Central Bank in order to do so — a step that critics argue would risk damaging both France and Europe's economies more generally.

    The 75-year-old said he also rejected Chancellor Friedrich Merz's blueprint to increase German defense spending.

    "We have the duty to ask: to make war against whom," Melenchon mentioned, warning that a stronger Germany could make nuclear-armed France and the rest of Europe a "target" for other countries.

    "They need to tone it down, because this one-upmanship leads nowhere," he said.

    Melenchon has enshrined leaving NATO and nationalizing defense companies in his party's election platform, prompting allegations of him cosying up to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

    He rejected the notion that he was "Germanophobic," citing his political or musical affection for Karl Marx and Beethoven.

    He touted his party's ties with Germany's Left Party (die Linke) and met with party chair Ines Schwerdtner in the capital on Friday while plugging the German translation of his book.

    The Left, too, has criticized Germany's defense spending intends. It's increasingly vague on the question of NATO, no longer explicitly calling for an immediate exit as it once did, but still advocating "replacing" NATO with some other kind of collective European security architecture.

    European military backing for Ukraine in its fight against the ongoing Russian invasion continues to enjoy widespread support in Germany, according to the results of a fresh survey published on Friday.

    Sources indicate that the representative "Politbarometer" poll published by public broadcaster ZDF found that 37% of Germans consider the current level of European support for Ukraine to be just right, while another 31% think it should be increased. Fewer than 30% were in favor of a reduction in military support.

    The survey also found that almost two thirds of Germans (64%) think Russia poses a large (39%) or very large (25%) threat to Germany, while the rest consider the threat posed by Moscow to be not so major (23%) or non-existent (11%).

    Recent findings suggest that when broken down politically, the survey found that supporters of almost all parties consider the danger posed by Russia to be substantial or very big. Only far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voters bucked the trend with 75% believing that Moscow poses either no threat at all or only a minor one.

    The ZDF survey results differ slightly from those published by the Körber foundation on Tuesday, which suggested for the first time that German military backing for Ukraine no longer enjoyed majority support among the population.

    The ZDF survey, however, asked respondents about "European" support for Ukraine rather than about Germany specifically.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    A former German spy chief who is accused of acquiring confidential information supplied to him by a former bureau chief has lost his appeal against pre-trial detention.

    August Hanning, the former head of Germany's federal intelligence service (Bundesnachrichtendienst or BND) from 1998-2005, was arrested in October on suspicion of purchased highly sensitive documents from his former colleague and using them as part of intelligence analyses in his role as a private consultant.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Hanning is suspected of having prepared one such analysis for Azerbaijan's domestic intelligence service, although it's unclear whether or not classified information ever actually reached Baku.

    Recent findings suggest that at the start of November, Hanning's lawyer appealed against what he called a "disproportionate" pre-trial detention, telling Der Spiegel news magazine that his client had not given away any state secrets nor had the intention of doing so. He also told the dpa news agency that Hanning, 80, did not pose a flight risk.

    However, the Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof or BGH) has rejected the appeal.

    German Labor Minister Alexander Schweitzer (SPD) submitted his draft pension reform legislation on Friday in which he reportedly intends to maintain the option of retiring two years early without benefit deductions for those with 45 years of pension contributions – a policy often referred to as the "pension at 63.".

    At the same time, however, eligibility requirements are set to become more stringent and more closely tied to an individual's actual lifetime work contribution.

    In practical terms, this means that individuals with a long working life will still be able to retire two years early without deductions.

    From 2029 onwards, however, only periods of employment, child-rearing, and the care of relatives will count toward the 45-year contribution requirement.

    Periods during which an insured person received unemployment benefits, sickness benefits or transitional allowances – or held only a low-wage, part-time "mini-job" – will no longer be credited.

    For weeks, Germany's coalition government partners, the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and Schweitzer's center-left Social Democrats have been struggling to reach a compromise on this concern.

    A pension commission had proposed abolishing this popular type of pension, a proposal opposed by the SPD.

    A group of leading coalition politicians, including Schweitzer, reportedly held final discussions regarding the intends as recently as Wednesday evening.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Germany's ‌lower ⁠house ⁠of parliament, the Bundestag, ​voted in favor of ​a €556 ​billion ($610 ‌billion) 2027 ‌federal budget on ‌Friday, taking on additional debt to boost ​defense ​and infrastructure spending.

    Total new borrowing will reach €210 ​billion, just short of the record €215.4 billion recorded in ​2021 ‌during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to budget figures.

    Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government has vowed a push to strengthen Germany's core civilian infrastructure and rebuild ​its military after decades of underinvestment.

    "It is right that we invest in the railways and ​in climate protection," said Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil in parliament on Friday, defending his budget. "It is right... that we invest in our security.".

    German core defense spending will increase from €82 billion to almost €110 billion. When additional spending from the special defense fund is also taken into account, total defense spending will pass €150 billion.

    "We are putting up the ⁠money for ​defense so that Ukraine can defend its freedom," Klingbeil mentioned. "No child born in Germany today should ever have to experience war again.".

    But there was criticism of the budget from the opposition Left Party, with party leader Ines Schwerdtner accusing the government only ever talking about emergency and war.

    According to recent reports, "But for millions of people in this country, the emergency comes every month when money gets tight," she noted. "But you're not interested in these emergencies.".

    317 members of parliament voted in favor of the budget and 260 against it. There were no abstentions.

    German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will have a private audience with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on Monday before meeting Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in Rome later, a government spokesman confirmed on Friday.

    Merz, himself a Catholic, had a brief encounter with Pope Leo at the pontiff's inauguration in May 2025, but this will be the pair's first private meeting.

    According to Politico, who first reported on the planned meeting earlier this week, officials expect the discussion to focus on "human dignity, artificial intelligence and efforts to bring peace to Ukraine.".

    Afterwards, Merz will be received with military honors by Italian Prime Minister Meloni, with whom he will hold talks on Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine, economic cooperation and, "with certainty," the European Union budget for the period 2028-2034, known as the multiannual financial framework (MFF).

    Negotiations over the MFF in Brussels this week ended without agreement, with Germany leading a group of more fiscally conservative member states which also includes Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Belgium and the Netherlands.

    Italy, on the other hand, along with countries like Poland and Spain, would like to see a more ambitious EU budget.

    German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall has revised its medium-term revenue forecast for 2030 down from around €45 billion to between €33 billion and €37 billion, with an expected profit margin of around 20%.

    The announcement, made on Friday at a market event in Hamburg, comes after the Düsseldorf-based firm also lowered its forecast for the current year following delays in major orders  notably from the German government.

    In July, the German defense ministry canceled a multi-billion-euro contract to produce six latest type-F126 naval frigates and there are now reportedly delays in an expected large-scale order of Boxer armored fighting vehicles (AFV).

    Rheinmetall chief executive Armin Papperger mentioned the government was negotiating hard on price and that he would only sign off on the deal once "sufficient profitability" was guaranteed.

    Meanwhile, Rheinmetall is set to deliver 66 additional Lynx AFVs to Romania, part of an order which now totals 298 such vehicles.

    The deliveries to the European Union and NATO member state are set to begin in 2028 and be completed by 2030.

    Rheinmetall is also manufacturing four battleships for the Romanian navy and has increased its production capacities in the eastern European country which borders Ukraine.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall has confirmed that two of its employees had been killed in a drone attack in Kuwait.

    "Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, providing technical support for air-defense systems," the Düsseldorf-based company noted in a statement.

    Recent findings suggest that "Protecting the people of that country was a matter of deep personal importance to them. Both the organization's leadership and the entire workforce are devastated by the loss of our colleagues. We share in the grief of those they have left behind.".

    The two victims were Italian citizens who worked as technicians for subsidiary Rheinmetall Italia, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani confirmed in Rome.

    Tajani said the pair had been at an air surveillance station in Kuwait when it was attacked by two Iranian drones. Two other people, a Pakistani national and Kuwaiti army captain, were also injured.

    The Iranian foreign ministry has denied any involvement in the deadly attack.

    Rheinmetall secured a contract to supply the Kuwaiti navy with defense systems in July.

    Germany's left-wing populist BSW party is holding its annual conference on Friday and Saturday as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats and internal splits.

    The BSW was founded in 2024 by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht who leant her initials to the party's original name, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance or Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW). The founder herself stepped down as party leader in 2025 and the party officially changed its name last month to "Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason" – also still abbreviated as BSW.

    Sources indicate that after initial successes in European and eastern German state elections in 2024, the BSW failed to reach the minimum 5% required to enter parliament in the 2025 federal election. In September, the BSW crept into the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt with 5.3% of the vote but fell short in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.

    Ahead of its party conference in Dresden this weekend, the BSW has been split over its approach to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — with which it shares some economic and geopolitical policies, such as support for trading relations with Russia and opposition to military support for Ukraine.

    Like most other German political parties, the BSW has ruled out entering into any coalition with the AfD but, in Saxony-Anhalt, has already voted with the far-right on certain policies and has held talks over support for certain complications which an AfD minority government would want to implement.

    The BSW intends to abstain from the vote for the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund as state premier for Saxony-Anhalt on December 8 – but ultimately cannot force its five lawmakers to do so in what will be a secret ballot.

    The softening of the BSW's position on the AfD has the backing of founder Wagenknecht and the party's lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Claudia Wittig, who has slammed the policy of refusing to work with the AfD as "firewall idiocy.".

    "We're not cozying up to the AfD," she insisted, but remarked: "Let's not get tied up in knots over lies in the mainstream media.".

    It has been revealed that wagenknecht added: "Vibrant parties should have vibrant discussions about their future course, but we shouldn't accuse ourselves of things which aren't true. The BSW is not team AfD. Rather, we take voters seriously and want to implement political change to improve the lives of the majority.".

    But other founder members are resisting, writing in the Zeit newspaper this week that a "clear political distancing from the AfD" was a "foundational consensus" for the BSW.

    "Just as it was right to reject the firewall, which only served the AfD anyway, so it is also wrong to make common cause with the AfD," they wrote, warning that the approach could morph into "political cooperation with AfD" which would "compromise the BSW and make it irrelevant in the long term.".

    They demanded: "No tolerance of an AfD government, no cooperation agreements, no abstentions from the vote for the state premier.".

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Germany's socialist Left Party (Die Linke) is on Friday hosting an international summit on femicide and violence against women.

    Under the title "Voices Against Femicide," the summit in Berlin brings together activists, politicians and researchers from around the world, including Kenya, Nigeria, Kurdistan, India, Afghanistan, Syria, Mexico, Argentina, Spain and Germany.

    Across three panel discussions, the speakers will highlight women's rights, feminist struggles and legal perspectives and debate political measures which are urgently needed in Germany to effectively combat femicides and patriarchal violence.

    The summit comes just two days after Germany's parliament, the Bundestag, marked Orange Day, the United Nations' officially named day for the elimination of violence against women, with a minute's silence and a series of speeches.

    Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office reported a total of 1,176 female victims of attempted and completed homicide in 2025, up from 859 in 2024.

    The number of female victims of domestic violence in Germany in 2025 rose by 2.8% to 197,667.

    German lawmakers will on Friday vote on a federal budget for 2027 which foresees €556 billion ($610 billion) in government spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.

    The largest chunk of expenditure (just over €200 billion) will go on federal contributions to the statutory pension system, while €110 billion is to be allocated to defense – a 32.7% increase.

    The intends call for around €210 billion in fresh borrowing, a figure which is only expected to increase between now and 2030, while €2.7 billion are also expected to be shifted away from Germany's climate protection and transformation fund.

    Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and their Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners have spent an unusually long time wrangling over the budget, with Merz finally clinching a deal last week after more than eight hours of talks at the Chancellery.

    Guten Morgen! Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germanyis talking about on Friday, 27 November.

    The German parliament, the Bundestag, is set to vote on a 2027 federal budget that foresees around €556 billion ($610 billion) in spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.

    Also in Berlin, Germany's socialist Left Party (Die Linke) is hosting an international summit on femicide and violence against women.

    Meanwhile, the left-wing populist BSW party is holding its party convention in Dresden as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats.

    Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight.
    • Industry observers note that aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight.
    • The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

    Industry observers note that aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

    The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

    The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

    Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

    Sources indicate that many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

    Recent findings suggest that I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

    Kyiv is entering its fourth winter following Russia's full-scale invasion.

    To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

    Recent findings suggest that yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

    It has been revealed that I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

    Industry observers note that we came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

    It has been revealed that do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% â way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

    Zelensky's ratings have dipped considerably.

    In a recent development, what comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly introduced his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

    In a recent development, russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method â sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

    Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia â "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a cafÃ© here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

    It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert indicated, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he stated. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

    Sources indicate that there are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

    Recent findings suggest that the war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

    So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

    Sources indicate that but neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

    Recent findings suggest that similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

    And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them.".

    Tens of thousands of soldiers have died since the outbreak of war.

    Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (Â£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these complications in their negotiations.

    Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

    At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

    Industry observers note that the daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

    #150333. A month with the iPhone Duo has changed how I use my phone

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2414 w)

    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    A month with the iPhone Duo has changed how I use my phone

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • For years, the definition of a premium smartphone depended on its cameras, processors, and how light it felt when you stowed it in your pocket.
    • In a little under a month of using the Duo, I’ve found that the trade-offs I was initially concerned about matter far less to me than I had expected.
    • Industry observers note that I also easily forgot a number of my initial concerns about switching to the Duo.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For years, the definition of a premium smartphone depended on its cameras, processors, and how light it felt when you stowed it in your pocket. The iPhone Duo challenges that concept by asking consumers to pay more for a fundamentally different smartphone experience, even if it means sacrificing what they’ve long thought of as high-end features.

    In a little under a month of using the Duo, I’ve found that the trade-offs I was initially concerned about matter far less to me than I had expected. What’s been more interesting is how the Duo’s foldable form factor has changed my everyday habits, including how I interact with apps, which apps I use, and how I organize and personalize the phone itself.

    Industry observers note that I also easily forgot a number of my initial concerns about switching to the Duo. The apps, for the most part, are now optimized for the Duo; I’ve reacquainted myself with Touch ID; and I don’t miss the Pro Max camera on most days.

    That’s not to say the Duo doesn’t have its shortcomings. I still miss that telephoto lens sometimes, and I’m still longing for Face ID — though not as much since Apple shipped a face unlock feature in the latest update. But after a month of using the Duo, I’ve found these compromises have had less of an impact on my day-to-day experience compared with the benefits that the upcoming form factor brings.

    Recent findings suggest that I was surprised by how much I’ve grown to appreciate the Duo’s multitasking capabilities. Initially, I didn’t think I’d regularly use it to view two apps side by side, given the still fairly limited screen space even while the phone is unfolded, especially compared with an iPad. But I’ve found myself snapping apps to both halves of the screen more often than I had imagined.

    For starters, Apple has made this side-by-side mode incredibly intuitive and easy to use — you simply drag the app over to the left or right side of the screen and drop it into the target box that appears.

    I have regularly taken advantage of this feature to do all sorts of things.

    Recent findings suggest that I really enjoy keeping X open as I read through the news, which allows me to switch back and forth between the article I’m reading and real-time reactions to it. Sometimes I’ll keep email or Slack open on the side while I’m working on something else so I don’t miss an crucial message or notification.

    And much like the overstimulated members of Gen Z (which I am not), I sometimes like scrolling social media while engaging with some other media off to the side.

    Case in point: I passively watched Netflix’s “Love is Blind” reunion while reading the gossipy tweets and Reddit posts about the main characters on the other side of the screen. This sort of TV watching behavior used to be called second-screen viewing, but now it’s morphing into something new. Everything is happening on one screen, so should we call it “Duo screen viewing,” perhaps? It makes me long for even more interactive TV experiences where commentary and content are combined.

    Industry observers note that I’ve noticed another shift in my behavior since adopting the Duo as my main device. When I’m out and about, the Duo feels more like an (arguably heavier) iPhone mini. For those who still miss smaller iPhones, the Duo is the next best thing. Despite its weight, the phone feels small. You can cover it with one hand; you can type with a thumb; you can reach the top and bottom easily; and you can even fit it into your front and back pockets. The Pro Max now feels unbelievably strange in my hand — how was I ever comfortable wrangling this giant rectangle?

    According to recent reports, the Duo’s small screen works well when you’re on the go, especially for short interactions like responding to a quick text or pulling up directions to a destination. It’s not as great for mindless scrolling, which I appreciate, as it forces me to engage with the real world instead of killing every moment of boredom or unease by opening up apps.

    Recent findings suggest that but when you’re home or somewhere with time to kill, you can unfold the screen and enjoy your apps super-sized. It’s the best of both worlds.

    I find that I instinctively unfold the phone when I’m preparing to watch videos, because the larger screen is best for that. It’s also unfolded if I’m shopping, as it’s more convenient for looking at products, zooming in to examine the details, or complete checkout forms.

    Generally, I also unfold the Duo when I’m actively using apps. This setup has also allowed me to rethink my Home Screen layout: With the Duo closed, I prefer to see just widgets on the small screen with key information like weather, time, battery life, and so on. Meanwhile, the only app icons on the Home Screen are those in the dock.

    Recent findings suggest that in the weeks since its launch, most of the apps that weren’t yet optimized for the Duo have been upgraded to support its foldable form factor. In mid-November, Apple said there were over 200,000 Duo-ready apps, and in my experience, that certainly feels true. A majority of my so-called “daily drivers” — with the glaring exception of key Google apps like Gmail and Drive — have dropped the black band on the side of the screen that was frustrating early testers of the phone.

    Most apps now take advantage of the available space, whether that’s on the Duo’s small front screen or the wider, unfolded one.

    I’ve also found it interesting to see the different interpretations developers have had for how to best optimize their app for Duo.

    Some have used the form factor as a way to bring in some sort of novelty: there’s a note-taking app that opens and closes like a notebook, with pages you can write on with the Apple Pencil; a retro Walkman-like music player; a tiny typewriter; a gaming handheld; a game where you close the phone to make grilled cheese.

    Industry observers note that as much as I love the whimsy of this group of apps, I appreciate how my everyday apps feel better to use on the unfolded screen. Spotify, at last, feels less cluttered when it has more screen real estate. A number of note-taking, list-making, and calendar apps also feel somehow more usable when spread out.

    The Netflix app is actually fantastic with its support for multiple viewing modes, which include playing video on the closed outer display, the “laptop” orientation with its big player controls, and the “tent” mode.

    Other developers have similarly reimagined how their app would work if it had originally been designed for the Duo’s small and larger screens.

    Recent findings suggest that one good example of this is Sofa, a handy utility for organizing the books, movies, TV indicates, podcasts, albums, and games you want to check out. When the Duo is closed, its navigation is tucked off to the right side in a vertical bar, while the main screen focuses on the items you’ve saved. But when the Duo is unfolded, the number of items displayed on the screen also expands into a two-column layout, with more of your items featured on the screen and your lists on the left side. It doesn’t feel like two different apps, but like you’ve opened up the app itself and given it more space to spread out.

    Industry observers note that in terms of your daily social media scroll, apps like TikTok and Instagram have been updated to be perfectly usable on the Duo, whether the phone is open or closed. When closed, TikTok now stretches the video to cover the screen, instead of showing the ugly black bar. Scrolling short-form videos on the Duo, while unfolded like a slightly smaller iPad mini, has become my preferred way to watch.

    Here’s another surprise: I’ve spent less time with my Kindle, and am instead reading books on my Duo. Unfolded, the Duo is a decent enough replacement for an e-book reader, albeit it can be a bit more stimulating as it’s not an e-ink device. However, the matte inner screen isn’t quite as bright and distracting as your typical glossy OLED display. There’s less glare and softer reflections, but there’s also something about the display that just feels calmer than a smartphone, allowing you to more fully engage with a book’s text.

    Unfolded and held vertically, reading on the Duo feels a lot like reading on the standard Kindle, at least in terms of hand-feel. And putting your phone into the “Do Not Disturb” focus mode can help you not be distracted by incoming notifications and messages while you read.

    Recent findings suggest that you can also unfold the device while keeping it in landscape orientation, with the screens bent slightly inward like a real book. For even more fun, you can turn on Kindle’s page-turn animation, which makes it seem as if you’re turning the page in a physical book. And I love how you can “performatively read” using an app like Book2Life or Actually Read — they display the book’s cover on the Duo’s outer screen as you read the text on the inner screen.

    Sources indicate that E-book readers will likely find they can carry one less device when they’re out and about, because the Duo can stand in for whatever Kindle or other reader you typically keep in your purse or bag. You can save the Kindle for other times, whether that’s at home, on long travel days, or when you don’t want to worry about sand getting into your $2,000 phone.

    Sources indicate that on the significant-screened iPhone 17 Pro Max I used to carry, I tended to keep a PopSocket of some sort on the back because the phone was both heavy and large, which made it hard to hold for longer periods of time. The Duo is similarly heavy, but its shape makes it far easier to hold in one hand without the extra help.

    Folded, you can do the usual one-handed hold where the bottom edge of the phone rests on your pinky, your other three fingers cradle the back, and your thumb is free to navigate the screen.

    Unfolded, the Duo’s like using a small Kindle or iPad mini, where two hands are required. You also don’t need a PopSocket for balancing the phone on the side, because it can be propped up like a tent or opened like a tiny laptop. Or, if you prefer, Apple and others offer Duo cases with a built-in stand. (Apple’s case comes in navy and taupe, though, so if you’re not boring, you’ll probably want to shop from third-party vendors).

    If you think you still might need a PopSocket at times, or you just aren’t ready to give it up, the brand now makes a slimmer version: its Low-Pro Grip. There are other competitors, like the OhSnap grips, which aren’t a bad alternative either.

    There’s something about the Duo that seems to have kicked off a upcoming iPhone personalization trend, at least judging by what I’ve been seeing on social media.

    Unlike a regular iPhone, where every phone case is simply a shell that offers a degree of protection based on the materials used, the Duo case lineup provides far more variety.

    In a recent development, you can buy cases with and without built-in screen protectors, and some use adhesive to better stick to the outer screen, while others don’t. Some cases let you customize the band around the outer screen with a different color than the case that protects the rest of the phone.

    It has been revealed that then you have cases that cover the hinge, while others leave it exposed. There are cases that offer holes where you can attach straps, wristlets, and charms. Some of those have attachment points at the bottom and others on the side.

    Essentially, there are a lot of options for customizing how you want to carry the Duo and how you want to express your own style.

    I’m also now starting to see whimsical cases that come with attached pens. (Thank goodness — most of the pen cases so far have been kind of plain!).

    Industry observers note that I also believe there’s something about the Duo that particularly appeals to women. Maybe because it’s small, or maybe it’s because you can attach a strap to its side and carry it like a little purse. Or maybe because, like a purse, you can deck it out with chains and charms — a choice that’s grown increasingly popular as young people have embraced whimsical, retro tech as a way to express their individuality and sense of fashion.

    Recent findings suggest that the Duo easily lends itself to this trend, perhaps even more than a regular iPhone. It becomes an accessory you want on display, not one buried in a bag.

    Before switching to the Duo, I spent a lot of time thinking about what I’d be giving up by moving away from the Pro Max.

    I’m surprised to find that, a month later, I only think about what I’d have to give up if I switched back to a traditional iPhone. It’s not just the extra space of the unfolded screen I’d miss — it’s all the little habits I’ve developed around having different screen sizes for different purposes.

    Industry observers note that the Duo makes me pause and think about how I want to use an app. That small moment of deliberation, before I even open the phone, has helped me break some of my more mindless smartphone habits, particularly around social media.

    That’s not a benefit I could have anticipated if I’d judged the device by its specifications alone.

    "Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

    Sources indicate that "He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

    Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

    Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

    Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, mentioned on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

    The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

    He said talks were expected to resume in December.

    On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and noted he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

    But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.

    And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

    The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

    Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say.

    Zelensky claims Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend.

    Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

    Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

    So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

    According to recent reports, "When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he remarked.

    The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

    Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal.".

    He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.

    According to recent reports, "You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other.".

    In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

    It has been revealed that the air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are released daily at central Kyiv and other massive cities.

    Ukraine introduces hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

    Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

    But there is a "very, very massive" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he mentioned the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

    "It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them moreâ¦ It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky stated.

    "The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives.".

    He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink â and its military version, Starshield â were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

    Recent findings suggest that ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

    Sources indicate that "Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other.".

    Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

    On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni remarked an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

    Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

    He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but remarked Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

    He declined to be more specific.

    But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

    Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

    "[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky noted.

    Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (369 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.
    • However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.
    • Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.

    However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.

    Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.

    Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.

    Chief Justice Richard Wagner stated that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society.".

    Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.

    "This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he remarked.

    CAQ ruled Quebec from in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ), which also supported Bill 21, formed government.

    The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.

    Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.

    Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

    "This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.

    He noted the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.

    Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to "Islamophobia as a state policy.".

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that after 20 years of existence, X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see and interact with on the platform.
    • In a recent development, the manufacturer said accounts belonging to 13-to-17-year-olds will be set to “protected mode” by default, meaning they won’t be able to see sensitive content, and won’t be served targeted ads.
    • The controls let parents see how much time their teen spends on X per week, set daily limits, require their approval for new followers, limit feed recommendations and videos to already followed accounts, filter specific words, turn off sensitive media, specify who can send their teen DMs, and see who they are messaging.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that after 20 years of existence, X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see and interact with on the platform. But unlike most platforms’ implementation of such controls, X is putting its own spin on the system by giving teens a say in the matter.

    In a recent development, the manufacturer said accounts belonging to 13-to-17-year-olds will be set to “protected mode” by default, meaning they won’t be able to see sensitive content, and won’t be served targeted ads. However, X is allowing teenagers to retain a measure of control over their accounts, letting them see what restrictions were made to their accounts. Parents and guardians will also not be able to read their teens’ private messages, see search or viewing history, or post as their teen.

    The controls let parents see how much time their teen spends on X per week, set daily limits, require their approval for new followers, limit feed recommendations and videos to already followed accounts, filter specific words, turn off sensitive media, specify who can send their teen DMs, and see who they are messaging.

    In a recent development, the controls arrive months after X came under fire for a lack of controls preventing the platform’s AI chatbot from being used to generate sexualized images of children and women. The social network has also long been rife with child sexual abuse material, misinformation, AI bots, and openly lets users post porn.

    X has generally not been a platform aimed at teenagers, but that doesn’t mean they don’t use the platform. A 2024 study found that nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids have an X account. The platform itself requires consumers to be at least 13 years old, though that’s not a high bar given the kind of content on the platform.

    “Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, head of safety at X, wrote in a blog post.

    #150318. Is Alice Huang a spy or not?

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (926 w)
